Listen to this article Share The invitation has arrived, and the first thought is often what to wear. Is there aso ebi to buy? How much will the tailor charge for the design? Will the shoes and bag in the wardrobe match the outfit, or will new ones be needed? Then comes the appointment for makeup, the gele, the hair and the accessories that will complete the look. Before the party begins, there is already a list of expenses to settle. For many Nigerian women, attending an owambe is an opportunity to dress up, experiment with fashion and put together an outfit that reflects their personal style. From the choice of fabric to the design of the dress and the accessories that bring everything together, getting ready can be just as exciting as the celebration itself. But that excitement can come at a price, particularly when wedding invitations arrive one after another. A woman who has just spent money on an outfit for one celebration may soon have another event to prepare for, with a different aso ebi, another tailoring fee and more money to set aside for beauty services. The spending can become even more noticeable when several events fall within the same month. There are clothes to buy, outfits to sew and appointments to keep, alongside the usual expenses of daily life. Even when each purchase seems reasonable on its own, the total can become substantial once everything is added together. For some women, the question is not whether they want to look good at an owambe, but how much they are willing or able to spend to achieve the look they want. While some enjoy investing in elaborate outfits for special occasions, others have to consider whether buying new clothes for every invitation is worth the expense. When the fabric is only the beginning The cost of dressing for an owambe extends beyond the price of aso ebi. Once the fabric has been purchased, the wearer must consider the cost of turning it into an outfit and completing the look. Consider a woman preparing for a wedding who spends N50,000 on aso ebi and another N20,000 on tailoring. She then spends N40,000 on shoes, a purse and jewellery, N27,000 on nails, N53,000 on makeup and N10,000 on transportation. By the time she is ready to leave for the event, she has spent N200,000, without accounting for other possible expenses such as hair styling, gele tying or money to spray at the party. The calculation shows how quickly the cost of a single outfit can rise. What begins as a purchase of fabric becomes a collection of expenses, each contributing to the final appearance. For women who attend several celebrations within a short period, the spending can accumulate. An outfit that costs N200,000 for one wedding could mean another substantial expense if the next invitation calls for a different fabric, a new design and additional beauty services. The challenge, therefore, is not only how much a woman spends on one occasion, but how often she has to repeat the process. The pressure to show up differently Aso ebi is more than fabric worn by guests at a Nigerian celebration. It helps identify family members, friends and other groups connected to the celebrant, making it an important part of the event’s visual identity. For guests, buying the designated fabric can be a way to show support and participate in the celebration. But the purchase is only one part of the preparation, particularly for women who want to coordinate the fabric with a carefully designed outfit, makeup and accessories. There is also the question of whether to repeat an outfit. Some women are comfortable wearing a dress to different occasions, while others prefer to create a different look for each event. Attending several celebrations involving the same friends and relatives can make that decision more noticeable, particularly when photographs are shared on social media. Yet the desire to dress well is not always about pressure. For many women, choosing an outfit, experimenting with styles and getting ready with friends are part of the enjoyment of an owambe. The clothes become a way to express personal taste while celebrating someone important to them. The difficulty arises when the cost of maintaining that appearance competes with other financial priorities. With several invitations arriving at once, women may have to decide which fabrics to buy, which events to attend and how much they can reasonably spend on each occasion. Making the wardrobe work harder For women who attend weddings regularly, managing the cost of looking good can require a change in how they approach their wardrobes. Rather than treating every invitation as a reason to purchase a complete new look, women can make existing clothes work for different occasions. A well-made outfit can be styled with different jewellery, bags, shoes or hairstyles, creating a fresh appearance without paying for an entirely new ensemble. Accessories can make a difference, particularly when the clothing itself is versatile enough to accommodate different combinations. A change of shoes, earrings or bag can alter the overall look without requiring another round of spending on fabric and tailoring. Women can also be selective about which aso ebi they buy, especially when several celebrations fall within the same month. Where the celebrant allows it, wearing an existing outfit in a suitable colour or style can be an alternative to purchasing new fabric. Planning ahead can also help. Setting a budget for the complete look, rather than considering each purchase separately, makes it easier to see how much an event will cost before committing to additional expenses. These choices do not have to mean abandoning personal style. They can instead help women decide which parts of their appearance matter most to them and where they can spend less without compromising the look they want. The people behind the look The cost of an owambe outfit also supports a network of businesses and service providers. Tailors, fashion designers, makeup artists, gele stylists, hairstylists and accessory sellers all contribute to the final appearance. Their services offer convenience, specialised skills and the finishing touches many guests want for important celebrations. However, prices can vary according to the complexity of a design, the materials used, the provider’s experience and the level of service requested. For customers, understanding these differences can help them decide where to spend more and where to make adjustments. A woman who wants an elaborate outfit may choose to allocate more money to tailoring, while another may prefer a simpler design and invest in makeup or accessories. Reducing costs does not always mean choosing the cheapest option. Reusing shoes and bags, planning outfits early and selecting designs that can be worn again may offer better value than repeatedly purchasing items for a single occasion. Looking good without overspending Owambe fashion remains an important part of how many Nigerians celebrate weddings, birthdays and other milestones. The clothes, colours and carefully assembled looks contribute to the atmosphere, giving guests an opportunity to express themselves while honouring the people hosting the events. But when celebrations come in quick succession, the cost of looking good can become difficult to manage. Each invitation brings a new decision about what to wear, what to buy and how much to spend. Some women may consider an elaborate outfit a worthwhile investment in their appearance and the celebration. Others may prefer to repeat clothes, change their accessories or reserve new purchases for occasions that matter most to them. Ultimately, looking good at every owambe does not have to mean starting from scratch each time. A wardrobe built around versatile pieces, thoughtful purchases and personal style can make it easier to enjoy the celebrations without allowing the pursuit of a new look to dictate every spending decision.
